info.title: uattest — Bongos API
info.description:
The Bongos API — the build-methodology backend
(builders, tasks, claims, credits, grading, memory).

**API version:** `v1` — served at `/api/bongos/v1`. The
unversioned `/api/bongos` and legacy `/api/gds` are permanent aliases
pinned to this version; pin to `/api/bongos/v1` for a stable
contract (breaking changes ship a new `/vN`, ADR 0117). This is the
CONTRACT version, distinct from the package build in `info.version`.

**Base path:** `/api/bongos` (every path below is relative to it).

**Auth:** a builder session — the `gds_session` cookie (web) or
`Authorization: Bearer <token>` (CLI). **Ranks** gate writes and are
enforced server-side per request, never cached (ADR 0016):
`public` < `any-builder` < `metic+archon` < `archon`.
Each operation carries its required rank in `x-rank`.

Generated from the live route files by `scripts/gds/gen-api-docs.js` —
do not hand-edit; it regenerates on every ship.

servers.description: Versioned API base (same-origin) — pin here for a stable contract.
Unversioned alias (permanent) — resolves to the current version.

get.description:
GET /access-requests?status=pending — the owner's queue. Defaults to pending; pass ?status=invited|dismissed for the resolved history. rank: archon — the queue exposes would-be builders' usernames. EVERY ROW SAYS WHETHER IT IS VOUCHED, and that is load-bearing rather than decoration (ADR 0201, Consequences). This endpoint is fed by the one PUBLIC unauthenticated write on the GDS, so anyone may file a request naming anyone — including a well-known builder. `vouched` is the reviewer's ONLY basis for reading a cross-project record beside a name: an unvouched row that LOOKED vouched is the entire impersonation vulnerability the vouch exists to close. It is derived here from `applicant_github_id IS NOT NULL` — the single mark (core_230) — rather than stored, so there is no second flag free to disagree with the identity it claims to describe. A VOUCH IS NOT AUTHORITY (ADR 0016). It says the hub confirmed WHO this is; it never says they may enter. Nothing on the approve path reads these three fields, and `hasInvitedAccessRequest` still reads status='invited' alone.

**Rank:** `archon` — Archon only (rank and identity management + the escalation keys — the trust boundary).

**Permissions:** `access_request.review` (all required).

post.description:
POST /access-requests — PUBLIC. A would-be builder asks to be admitted. rank: public — the requester is by definition outside the system (no builder row yet); this is the one public write on the GDS.

**Rank:** `public` — No authentication — any caller.

POST /access-requests/invite — an Archon admits a GitHub username BEFORE any request exists (task 1003044): the only way in on an invite-only project, where the public POST refuses, and a shortcut on an apply one. It writes the same access_request row the sign-in gate reads (status 'invited' — hasInvitedAccessRequest), so nothing new is consulted at sign-in; a pending request for that login is resolved in place rather than duplicated. Two Archons inviting the same login at once can each insert a row (the unique index covers pending only): harmless — the gate reads "any invited row" — and it shows as two lines in the invited history, so no lock is taken. A fresh row is marked kind='invite' with created_by = the sender (a rescind overwrites resolved_by) and the optional note as the inviter's words. A pending request resolved in place stays an application with its applicant's own note (ADR 0335 D2.1–D2.3; task 1002814). Every outcome that leaves the login invited also notifies the hub, so the invitee sees it in My Projects (ADR 0353). body: { github_login, note? }. 201 with a new row; 200 with the row when a pending request was resolved; 200 already_invited when an invite already stands; 409 already_member when they have an account. rank: archon — the same gate as resolving a request.

**Rank:** `archon` — Archon only (rank and identity management + the escalation keys — the trust boundary).

**Permissions:** `access_request.review` (all required).

get.description:
GET /access-requests/invites[?mine=1] — the outstanding invites: kind='invite', still 'invited' (not rescinded), and no builder row yet (not yet accepted by signing in), each naming its sender; ?mine=1 keeps only the caller's own (ADR 0335 D2; task 1002814). Rescind one with PATCH /access-requests/:id. Each carries `expires_at`, and `expired` once its 30 days are up (task 1002969): listed so the sender knows to invite again, and dropped once a newer invite for the same login is live, since that one already replaced it. rank: archon — it names logins that are not members yet.

**Rank:** `archon` — Archon only (rank and identity management + the escalation keys — the trust boundary).

**Permissions:** `access_request.review` (all required).

GET /access-requests/status?github_login=X — PUBLIC. The `bongos login` CLI polls this after filing a request: the device flow's not_approved is TERMINAL (the device_code is spent), so the CLI can't re-poll the flow — it polls this instead, then restarts sign-in once admitted. Exposes nothing the public POST above doesn't already reveal through its 409s (already_member / already_approved). status ∈ member | invited | expired | pending | dismissed | none; admitted = member||invited. `expired` is an invite past its 30 days (task 1002969): the door is shut, and the CLI stops waiting rather than polling a door that will not open. rank: public — a would-be builder is by definition outside the system. Declared BEFORE `GET /access-requests` so the literal `/status` path is matched as its own route (not swallowed as a query on the list route). RATE-LIMITED (task 1003339 / ADR 0209). Public + unthrottled, this was a login→membership oracle an attacker could script at line rate to learn who builds here. accountExistenceReadRateLimit is the doorway's SHARED 120/60s per-IP budget: core's GET /auth/web/admission-status (the boolean twin of this answer) mounts the very same instance, so the two cannot be alternated for double the rate. The limiter runs before the queries, so a refused probe costs no DB work. Whether the ANSWER should also collapse — so a caller who is not the subject cannot tell pending/dismissed/none apart — is the owner's call and is filed as a blocker, not decided here.

**Rank:** `public` — No authentication — any caller.

patch.description:
PATCH /access-requests/:id — the owner resolves a request. body: { status: 'invited' | 'dismissed' }. 'invited' = admitted (the only sign-in gate — no repo access needed); 'dismissed' = declined / spam / dup. The row stays as the audit trail either way. rank: archon — same gate as the rest of the roster management surface. THREE STATES, AND EVERY MOVE BETWEEN THEM THAT MEANS SOMETHING (ADR 0201 D4): pending → invited approve pending → dismissed decline invited → dismissed RESCIND (task 1002284, D4.2). An approval given by mistake, BEFORE the applicant has ever signed in, must be revocable: hasInvitedAccessRequest stops matching and the door re-locks. AFTER they have signed in the row is history, and this route REFUSES rather than flipping it. The refusal is the whole point: firstTimeAdmissionBlocked short-circuits on an existing `builders` row, so dismissing an invited row for someone who already signed in changes NOTHING about their access — it would answer 200 and let the queue report a removal that did not happen. Offboarding a member is the instance's own act (/builder-exit), and the guard is a NOT EXISTS in the UPDATE's own WHERE so it cannot be lost to a read-then-write window. KNOWN LIMIT: a rescind overwrites resolved_by/ resolved_at with the RESCINDER, so who originally approved is not recoverable from the row, and this route writes no audit_log for any transition (it never has — approve and decline lose nothing only because they start from `pending`, which has no resolver to lose). Carrying the prior approver out would mean a CTE on the one statement in this change that no engine executes in CI; it belongs with the queue UI that would display it (R11). ADR 0208. x → x IDEMPOTENT (D4.4). A double-clicked button in the queue returns the row it already holds, 200, rather than a 409 that reads as a failure. It does NOT re-stamp resolved_by/resolved_at: the audit trail records who ACTUALLY resolved it, not who clicked again afterwards. dismissed → invited REFUSED here on purpose. Re-admitting a declined applicant is POST /access-requests/invite, which already resolves-or-inserts an invited row for any login (D4.2) — a second path to the same write would be the drift. The refusal names the state and that route, per ADR 0116. The transition is enforced in the UPDATE's own WHERE, so a concurrent write loses the race in the database rather than in a read-then-write window. The follow-up SELECT runs ONLY to explain a refusal — it decides nothing. $1 is spelled $1::text in that WHERE because the same parameter is also the SET value. Postgres infers text from the assignment anyway, but no real engine ever executes this statement — there is no integration test for this route and CI has no Postgres — so the type is stated rather than relied on.

**Rank:** `archon` — Archon only (rank and identity management + the escalation keys — the trust boundary).

**Permissions:** `access_request.review` (all required).

get.description:
All seeded achievements — lets /builders render locked + unlocked side by side. rank: any-builder — global achievement catalog (locked + unlocked rendering).

**Rank:** `any-builder` — Any authenticated builder (row-level ownership enforced in-handler).

GET /agent-runs/:id — COLLECT THE ANSWER TO A FIRE YOU STARTED. OWN RUNS ONLY, enforced in the WHERE clause rather than after the read. The id is a sequential integer primary key, so without this any authenticated builder could walk the ledger and read another builder's held answer — text generated from THEIR free-text question, out of a repo the agent read — plus the github_login in `trigger_ref`. That is the textbook IDOR, and it is worse here than the usual shape because the interesting field is model output derived from someone else's prompt. Filtering in SQL, not in JS, is deliberate: a post-read comparison is one early `return` away from leaking, and it would still have handed the row to `hold.take()` on the way past. A run with a NULL requester (an event-triggered fire — nobody asked for it) is therefore readable by nobody here, which is correct for a route whose job is "collect MY answer". An operator's view of the whole ledger is a different surface with a different gate, and it is not built: when it is, it belongs behind `agent.arm`, not behind a widening of this route. See ../lib/answer-hold.js for why the text is held and not stored.

**Rank:** `any-builder` — Any authenticated builder (row-level ownership enforced in-handler).

GET /agents — the whole registry. Unpaginated on purpose: agents are instance CONFIGURATION reconciled from committed files, so the row count is bounded by what a human wrote, not by traffic. If that ever stops being true, this is the line that needs a cursor — not a silent LIMIT, which would make the registry quietly incomplete.

**Rank:** `any-builder` — Any authenticated builder (row-level ownership enforced in-handler).

post.description:
POST /agents — author a definition against the DB, no file edit. It lands DISARMED, always. Creating and arming are separate acts with separate audit lines, and a create that armed would let one call both invent an agent and switch it on — the same reasoning agents-sync rule 4 applies to a commit, applied to an HTTP request.

**Rank:** `metic+archon` — Metic or Archon rank (review/triage powers).

**Permissions:** `agent.author` (all required).

get.description:
GET /agents/:name — one definition, persona included. The name is validated against the SAME regex the schema CHECKs, before it reaches the query. The query is parameterised regardless, so this is not the injection wall — it is the difference between a 404 and a 400 for a caller who sent something that could never have been a name.

**Rank:** `any-builder` — Any authenticated builder (row-level ownership enforced in-handler).

patch.description:
PATCH /agents/:name — edit IN PLACE. One row per name, before and after. The patch is merged over the stored row and the WHOLE definition is re-validated (authoring.mergeForValidation says why), against the EDITOR's live rank — which re-stamps author_rank downward if a lower-ranked builder edits, and re-runs the scope wall against that new rank.

**Rank:** `metic+archon` — Metic or Archon rank (review/triage powers).

**Permissions:** `agent.author` (all required).

delete.description:
DELETE /agents/:name — only a db-authored definition, and only ever one. The LEDGER is untouched: agents_runs.definition_id is ON DELETE SET NULL and carries a denormalized agent_name, so what this agent spent and did survives the definition it pointed at (the schema header says why).

**Rank:** `metic+archon` — Metic or Archon rank (review/triage powers).

**Permissions:** `agent.author` (all required).

post.description:
POST /agents/:name/disable — and THIS is what stops dispatch. Two halves, because there are two ways an agent fires. The event dispatch index is partial (`WHERE enabled`), so an event agent switched off stops being selected at all; an on-demand agent has no selection step, so gate.js refuses it at invoke. Off means off on both paths, which is the property this route exists to give an operator.

**Rank:** `metic+archon` — Metic or Archon rank (review/triage powers).

**Permissions:** `agent.arm` (all required).

POST /agents/:name/enable — THE OPERATOR ACT. This is the one write that works on a FILE-sourced definition, and it is the whole reason a committed agent can ever run: agents-sync deliberately never arms anything (its rule 4), and carries an operator's `enabled` forward untouched on every later deploy. So arming here is durable, and landing a commit still cannot arm anything. Two refusals it cannot talk its way past, both enforced by the schema as well as here: a flagged definition stays disarmed, and a definition with no author_rank has no authority to act with.

**Rank:** `metic+archon` — Metic or Archon rank (review/triage powers).

**Permissions:** `agent.arm` (all required).

POST /agents/:name/invoke — fire an on-demand agent. 202, never 200. A fire takes 60-120 seconds and costs about a dollar, which is past the edge proxy's patience — so the ledger row IS the response and the run continues behind it. Collect the answer from GET /agent-runs/:id. SELF-GATED at requireBuilder, deliberately, matching the reads: which agents exist at all is an operator decision, and a v1 agent is hard-read-only. The thing that reasoning does NOT bound is SPEND, so a per-builder ceiling does (../lib/fire-budget.js). It is a blast radius, not a budget: the real accounting is agents_runs.cost_usd through the shared LLM cost cache.

**Rank:** `any-builder` — Any authenticated builder (row-level ownership enforced in-handler).

get.description:
a builder's historical AI dev curve. A builder reads their own id; an Archon reads anyone's (powers the cross-builder view).

**Rank:** `any-builder` — Any authenticated builder (row-level ownership enforced in-handler).

GET /artist-gate — this project's artist strictness and what it is holding. rank: any authenticated builder. The payload is ordinary board state — a policy value the instance already publishes as its own behaviour, and task ids/titles any builder can read on the hall — so a floor above requireBuilder would gate a fact the board already shows. Nothing here is writable. Response: mode 'off' | 'advisory' | 'strict' the project's setting as resolved since ISO string | null when it was last RAISED to strict holds boolean does anything hold a deploy now? truncated boolean `reviews` hit the scan cap — a floor reviews [{ id, created_at }] the open reviews that count halt { code, message, detail } | null the refusal, pre-composed `halt` is composed HERE rather than by the caller on purpose: ADR 0241 §4's second guard is that the refusal must name what holds the deploy and which control releases it, and a sentence assembled independently by each caller is a sentence that eventually says something different. One composer, one wording. A caller on this machine that reached the app DIRECTLY may also read it, without a session (task 1004205; owner decision 2026-09-23): that is how `bongos upgrade` on the box asks before moving the pin, and the box holds no builder session. Everything else still passes requireBuilder.

**Rank:** `any-builder` — Any authenticated builder (row-level ownership enforced in-handler).

GET /api/bongos/audit-log?limit=&offset=&builder_id=&method= Paginated, newest-first. Clamps: limit → 1..500, default 100 offset → >= 0, default 0 rank: archon — forensics surface; only the Archon should see who did what. Gate: requirePermission('audit_log.read') — BV1.R104; the seeded rank-role makes the permission and the old rank floor identical (ADR 0151).

**Rank:** `metic+archon` — Metic or Archon rank (review/triage powers).

**Permissions:** `audit_log.read` (all required).

post.description:
POST /auth/backchannel-logout — the INSTANCE side of federated single-logout (ADR 0144, task 1002238). The hub POSTs a hub-signed logout token here when a builder signs out of the hub; we verify it and revoke ALL of that builder's local sessions, so one hub logout ends the session on every federated project. rank: public — the hub-signed EdDSA logout token IS the credential (like the OAuth callback), NOT a builder session. Inert (404) on an instance that does not federate through a hub (idp unset), so a self-hosted instance exposes no new surface. Idempotent: an unknown/replayed subject just revokes nothing.

**Rank:** `public` — No authentication — any caller.

POST /auth/cli-token/issue — V3.R91 / task 401. Issue a fresh CLI bearer for the requesting builder, gated on a WEB COOKIE session (not a bearer). The browser already proves identity via the gds_session cookie; this endpoint mints a separate cli-source session row the builder can paste into ~/.config/otb/gds-session.json via `bongos paste-token`. Replaces the ~30-60s Device Flow when the CLI bearer has expired. rank: any-builder (own identity only) — no rank gate. auth source restriction: cookie ONLY. A bearer cannot mint a new bearer (a leaked CLI token shouldn't be able to extend its own lifetime; the httpOnly browser cookie is the harder-to-steal credential).

**Rank:** `any-builder` — Any authenticated builder (row-level ownership enforced in-handler).

POST /auth/device/exchange — CLI federation (ADR 0141 §1). The CLI ran the device flow against the HUB and got a hub-signed assertion; it presents it here. The instance verifies the Ed25519 signature OFFLINE against the provisioned hub public key (aud must equal this instance's client_id, unexpired), then runs the instance's OWN admission gate + upsertBuilder + createSession(source='cli') and returns the existing { token, builder }. Only reachable when auth.idp is set. rank: public — an auth-establishment endpoint; the hub-signed assertion IS the bearer and is cryptographically verified before any session is minted.

**Rank:** `public` — No authentication — any caller.

completes the link to the caller's own identity.

**Rank:** `any-builder` — Any authenticated builder (row-level ownership enforced in-handler).

/auth/discord — account-linking OAuth (Phase 3 F2, ADR 0033 §2). Links a Discord account to the ALREADY-AUTHENTICATED builder (gds_session cookie): the link is self-asserted by the builder, never invented by the bot. Inert (503) until the server has Discord client creds. Mirrors the GitHub web flow's CSRF-state discipline above — a hard requirement (ADR 0033 §2). rank: any-builder — links to your OWN identity; no rank gate.

**Rank:** `any-builder` — Any authenticated builder (row-level ownership enforced in-handler).

unlink your OWN Discord. JSON (called from the hall UI). F7 follow-up: also kicks the builder from the guild so they can't remain in the server without a linked account. The kick is best-effort — the unlink always succeeds even if the bot lacks Kick Members or the member already left.

POST /auth/revoke — V3.R38 / task 259. Archon-only. Kill a SINGLE session by its primary-key id. Used for surgical lockouts (e.g. a compromised CLI on a known builder's laptop) without disturbing that builder's other sessions. Body: { session_id: <bigint> }. Response: { ok, revoked: 0|1 }. rank: archon — kills an arbitrary session; can lock other builders out. Gate: requirePermission('auth.session.revoke') — BV1.R104; the seeded rank-role makes the permission and the old rank floor identical (ADR 0151).

**Rank:** `archon` — Archon only (rank and identity management + the escalation keys — the trust boundary).

**Permissions:** `auth.session.revoke` (all required).

POST /auth/revoke-all — V3.R38 / task 259. Archon-only. Kill EVERY active session for a given builder. Used at demotion (auto-called from setBuilderRank when newRank moves down the ladder — C7 rank-change-near- instant) and as a manual operator hammer. Body: { builder_id: <bigint> }. Response: { ok, revoked: <count> }. rank: archon — same authority as PATCH /builders/:id/rank. Gate: requirePermission('auth.session.revoke') — BV1.R104; the same atom /auth/revoke gates on (ADR 0151).

**Rank:** `archon` — Archon only (rank and identity management + the escalation keys — the trust boundary).

**Permissions:** `auth.session.revoke` (all required).

get.description:
GET /auth/web/admission-status?login=X — the probe renderAccessPendingPage polls (task 1002097). Answers ONE question: would this login be admitted right now? It mirrors the real gate via auth.webAdmissionStatus so the page can never invite someone in the gate would refuse. rank: public — it must be reachable by a visitor with no session (that is the entire situation it exists for). It grants nothing: admission still runs through the normal sign-in, and this only reads state. WHAT IT LEAKS, stated plainly (task 1002430 — an earlier version of this comment claimed the opposite and was wrong). Returning only a boolean does NOT make it non-enumerable: with open enrollment off, and for any login that is not the configured firstAdmin, `admitted:true` means that login is a member or has been invited. That reveals account existence to an unauthenticated caller. IT IS NOW THROTTLED (task 1003339 / ADR 0209). It used to say "NOT throttled" here, and that was true: rateLimitMiddleware returns early for non-write methods, so GETs bypassed it entirely and the page's 3s poll bounded the honest client, not an attacker. accountExistenceReadRateLimit below is the ceiling — 120 reads/60s per IP, and the SAME instance is mounted on the onboarding module's GET /access-requests/status, which is this route's strictly richer twin (member|invited|pending|dismissed|none plus its own `admitted`). One budget across both, because they are one oracle: hardening either alone would accomplish nothing, and giving each its own budget would just let an enumerator alternate for double the rate. WHAT IS STILL OPEN and is deliberately NOT decided here: whether the answer itself should collapse, so a caller who is not the subject cannot tell pending/dismissed/none apart from a bare "not admitted". That changes what a real invited user sees during onboarding, so it is the owner's call — filed as a blocker against task 1003339, not settled by a comment in this file. That endpoint is also why this one exists: it models neither the firstAdmin bypass nor open enrollment, so it reports the OWNER as 'none' forever — the exact case this page has to resolve.

**Rank:** `public` — No authentication — any caller.

OAuth callback; the state cookie + code are the bearer.

**Rank:** `public` — No authentication — any caller.

GET /auth/web/handoff?code=&return= — the far side of the one-time session handoff (task 1004357). The canonical host minted `code` for THIS host after a sign-in (or for a builder already signed in there); trading it sets this host's own host-only copy of the session, then lands on `return` — a relative path only, so the handoff can never become an open redirect. rank: public — auth establishment; the one-time code is the bearer, bound to this exact host, single-use and alive for HANDOFF_TTL_MS.

**Rank:** `public` — No authentication — any caller.

/auth/web — browser flow (used by the /builders page). rank: public — entry into the GitHub OAuth handshake.

**Rank:** `public` — No authentication — any caller.

post.description:
The owner pauses or resumes ONE builder's runner without throwing the master switch. Same atom as the kill switch: stopping a machine is the same act whether it is everyone's or one person's, and the paused builder must not be able to lift it (autonomy.run does not reach this route).

**Rank:** `archon` — Archon only (rank and identity management + the escalation keys — the trust boundary).

**Permissions:** `autonomy.fence.manage` (all required).

get.description:
The runner's own read, every iteration. ANY-BUILDER on purpose: learning that you must stop should never require an elevated session, because the failure mode of "could not read the fence" is a machine that keeps going. The body carries no secret — it is a boolean, a reason string and a list of goal ids. THE CALLER'S fence, not the project's (task 1004501). The top-level `enabled` and `goals` are what THIS builder's runner may do: the project switch, then `autonomy.run`, then the owner's pause on this builder, and the allowlist narrowed to their own picks (fence.js effectiveFence). Computing it here keeps the runner dumb and means a runner that predates this change is narrowed too. The unnarrowed project fence rides along as `project` for the owner's page.

**Rank:** `any-builder` — Any authenticated builder (row-level ownership enforced in-handler).

post.description:
The kill switch. Archon, system:true — see the catalog entry for why it is the one permission that cannot be delegated to a custom rank.

**Rank:** `archon` — Archon only (rank and identity management + the escalation keys — the trust boundary).

**Permissions:** `autonomy.fence.manage` (all required).

delete.description:
Revoke one. `removed` distinguishes "just revoked" from "already gone" — an owner clicking Remove deserves to know which happened.

**Rank:** `archon` — Archon only (rank and identity management + the escalation keys — the trust boundary).

post.description:
The priority goal (task 1004453): which allowlisted goal the runner works first. Same gate as the allowlist — choosing what an unattended machine does first is part of choosing what it may do. The goal must already be on the allowlist (409 otherwise), so a priority can order the list and never widen it. `goal_id: null` clears it.

**Rank:** `archon` — Archon only (rank and identity management + the escalation keys — the trust boundary).

**Permissions:** `autonomy.fence.manage` (all required).

The runner's check-in, once per loop. ANY-BUILDER is safe because the row is keyed by the CALLER: a stranger reporting "winbox" writes their own row and cannot touch the owner's, so the liveness signal cannot be forged into reading alive. Keeping the bar low matters — the failure mode of a refused heartbeat is a healthy runner reported dead.

**Rank:** `any-builder` — Any authenticated builder (row-level ownership enforced in-handler).

put.description:
A builder picks which allowlisted goals THEIR runner works. Replaces the whole list; `[]` means "my runner takes no work". Keyed by the session, never the body, so nobody can set another builder's picks. Behind `autonomy.run`: a builder who may not run a runner has nothing to scope. A goal not on the project allowlist is refused with 409 and nothing is written — the pick can narrow the project fence and never widen it.

**Rank:** `metic+archon` — Metic or Archon rank (review/triage powers).

**Permissions:** `autonomy.run` (all required).

**Rank:** `metic+archon` — Metic or Archon rank (review/triage powers).

**Permissions:** `autonomy.precheck` (all required).

What the hall renders: the CALLER'S OWN runners, with the pure verdict attached so the page and any future alert cannot disagree about what "dead" means. A row names a machine, its hostname and a pid — the caller's infrastructure, and nobody else's business.

**Rank:** `any-builder` — Any authenticated builder (row-level ownership enforced in-handler).

The owner's view of every builder's runners: who, which goals they picked, whether they are paused, and each runner's health — the server's verdict, as GET /autonomy/runners attaches it. Owner-only: a heartbeat names a machine and its hostname, which is each builder's own business (task 1003905), and the owner is the one person who needs every row to run the fence.

**Rank:** `archon` — Archon only (rank and identity management + the escalation keys — the trust boundary).

**Permissions:** `autonomy.fence.manage` (all required).

READ-ONLY and behind the SAME atom as the precheck above (`autonomy.precheck`, Metic+): whoever may ask the gate the question may read its past answers, and a new atom would need a migration for no change in audience. Adds no gate anywhere — pure observability over rows the precheck already writes. ?routine=<name> narrows to one routine; ?limit=1..100 (default 20), newest first.

patch.description:
PATCH /done-when/:criterionId — amend a criterion's TEXT (task 1003102) and/or MOVE it between goals (task 1003509). Was write-once: this file exposed create, satisfy and unsatisfy and nothing else, so wrong text had no API repair path. The incident that forced it: a shell-quoting error stripped backtick-wrapped literals out of three criteria on goal 1000073 at CREATION time — the intent was recorded, the text was wrong, and the only channels were prod SQL or archiving the goal (worse: criteria are version-level rows, so an archived goal's criteria linger in the version rollup). A SATISFIED criterion is REFUSED, by name — see prose-edits.criterionProseRefusal for why that is a decision and not a limitation: a satisfied criterion is a claim someone verified, and re-wording it re-points that verification at text nobody checked. Unsatisfy → edit → re-satisfy makes the undo a recorded act. Gated like criterion CREATION — BOTH HALVES. The permission `criterion.create` is only the RANK floor; the sibling POST /versions/:id/done-when also runs authorizeCriterionCreate, the per-goal owner|manager wall (ADR 0154). Copying just the rank half would let any Metic rewrite criteria on a goal they neither own, manage, nor belong to — reusing the SAME pure gate is the only way the claim "gated like creation" is true. (Caught by the grader on the first cut of task 1003102: the comment said it, the code did half of it.) rank: metic+archon — matches POST /versions/:id/done-when. THE GOAL MOVE (task 1003509 — walk finding W5). `goal_id` used to be writable only by createCriterion's INSERT, so a criterion was born linked and stayed that way for life. The runner seeds a fresh instance's V1 criterion with NO goal — at standup there is no goal yet to name (provision-repo.js seedFirstVersionCmd) — so the owner's first goal could never adopt it: /progress showed the criterion "(ungrouped)" forever beside the goal it obviously belonged to, reporting `criteria: []`. Amending it took SQL, and a hub-provisioned owner has no SQL access at all. BOTH ENDS OF A MOVE ARE GATED, not just the goal it leaves. A move is a criterion write on the DESTINATION every bit as much as on the source, and gating only the source would let a goal's own owner push their criterion into a goal they have no authority over — a criterion being, per the CREATE route above, a thing that permanently blocks version close and goal auto-achieve with no delete route to undo it. So authorizeCriterionCreate runs against both and both must pass. DETACH (`goal_id: null`) has no destination, so it lands on that gate's goal-less branch and is Archon-only — the same wall that makes version-level criteria Archon-only at creation (ADR 0154), reached without a rule of its own. A SATISFIED criterion may still MOVE. criterionProseRefusal freezes the text of a verified claim, and that reasoning is about re-wording: moving one between goals changes how it is grouped, never what was checked. It is refused here only when the prose is what is changing. WHO CAN ADOPT THE SEEDED CRITERION. Because a goal-LESS criterion is version-level, the source gate's own goal-less branch makes ANY write to one Archon-only — which predates this task (a non-Archon could not edit an ungrouped criterion's prose either). That is not a wall in front of W5: the founder of a wizard-born instance IS its Archon, so the one criterion this was filed for is theirs to place. A Metic is unaffected where it matters — regrouping between two goals they already hold needs no escalation.

**Rank:** `metic+archon` — Metic or Archon rank (review/triage powers).

**Permissions:** `criterion.create` (all required).

The pickup half of the handoff R144 and R145 set up: the author consented by marking the spark, the queue made it findable, and now another builder fills in the five template fields and the thought becomes a Full Idea. OPEN TO ANY BUILDER, INCLUDING THE AUTHOR. Cross-builder development is the entire point, so there is no author check here — the mirror image of R144, where the gate was the whole feature. The consent was already given and is already recorded (this row is a spark BECAUSE its author said so), and re-asking for it would make the queue unpickable. Self-development is likewise legal: an author may mark a thought and come back to it themselves. ONLY A SPARK CAN BE DEVELOPED, and "only once" is enforced by the DATABASE, not by this handler. developSpark's UPDATE carries `AND grade = 'spark'`, so two builders picking the same spark off the queue at the same instant cannot both succeed — the second matches zero rows. The pre-read below exists ONLY to tell a 404 apart from a 409 and to give a useful message; it is not the guard, and it deliberately does not try to be. THE STREAM-2 CREDIT IS PAID HERE, SPLIT (task 1002923 / R147, ADR 0185). R146 shipped this route paying nothing on purpose: with two people involved, the recipient was ambiguous, and awardIdeaFullPassCredit's idempotency predicate is (builder_id, reason) — so guessing the developer would NOT have blocked a later payment to the author, and one idea would have paid twice. R147 resolved that by moving the payee decision INTO the economy module: it reads captured_by + developed_by itself and books 70% to the developer, 30% to the spark author (one payee at 100% when they are the same person). This route can therefore call it safely — it no longer chooses who earns. The board window IS opened, because it is recipient-agnostic (it takes an idea and a score, not a builder) and without it a developed Full Idea could never reach ratification — the handoff would dead-end one step from done. Fail-open like every other caller of that port. rank: any-builder — development is the pickup, and the author's mark is the consent. The kind='criterion-proposal' POST is Metic+ (gated above), but the ratification is the Archon decision. Returns 400 if the source idea isn't kind='criterion-proposal' or its body_md isn't a parseable {target_version, criterion_md, sort_order_hint} JSON object. Returns 404 if the idea doesn't exist. Returns 409 if the idea is already promoted/discarded/merged (status != 'open'). All four writes happen in one transaction — partial failures roll back cleanly.

post.description:
----------------------------------------------------------------------- BFG CROSS-BUILDER WRITE (task 446 / ADR 0026 §6C) — the FIRST cross-builder memory write path, the deliberate bounded exception to ADR 0016. Reachable ONLY by the BFG service principal (requireBfgPrincipal — an IDENTITY gate on system_role='bfg', NOT a rank gate, so an Archon/stolen token is rejected), ONLY when the kill-switch BFG_WRITE_ENABLED is on, and EVERY write lands a fail-closed audit row in the SAME transaction as the write (memory.bfgWrite- MemoryFile). Writes are namespaced (bfg/<kind>-<slug>.md) + self-announcing (frontmatter author: BFG) so a BFG note can never masquerade as the builder's own. The builder can always see and delete it. Unlike /memory/sync — which carries up to 50 MB and needed a tighter dedicated cap — this endpoint doesn't warrant its own limiter, especially as it's principal-only + kill-switched. POST /memory/builders/:builderId/bfg-write body: { kind: 'dream'|'correction', slug, title?, body_md, rationale } 201 → { ok, builder_id, path, kind, author:'BFG', audit_id, sha256, byte_len, updated_at } Declaration opener kept on ONE line (route path beside router.post) so the deterministic route-rank auditor (src/bongos/route-rank-check.js) detects + classifies it; it reads requireBuilder in the chain below → 'any-builder', and requireBfgPrincipal narrows that to the principal alone.

post.description:
POST /memory/sync — push a builder's local memory files to the server. Auth: any authenticated builder (requireBuilder). A builder can only ever write their OWN memory — the owner is req.builder.id, never from input. Request body (two accepted shapes): { files: [ { path, content, mtime? }, ... ] } (preferred) [ { path, content, mtime? }, ... ] (bare array, also ok) where: path — string, relative path under the memory dir (e.g. 'MEMORY.md'). Validated by storeMemoryFile (no leading '/', no '..', no NUL). content — string, the file body (UTF-8). mtime — optional ISO-8601 string or epoch ms; the source file's mtime. Stored for the pull side's newer-than check. Server clock is the conflict authority (last-write-wins), so this is advisory. Response 200 (always 200 when the request itself was well-formed; per-file outcomes are in the body so one bad file doesn't sink the batch): { stored: <count of files upserted>, skipped: <count of files skipped — e.g. non-string content>, errors: [ { path, code, message, hint? }, ... ], results: [ { path, stored: true, sha256, byte_len, updated_at } | { path, error: {...} } ] } A quota/oversize failure on a file is reported in errors[] with code FILE_TOO_LARGE / MEMORY_QUOTA_EXCEEDED and an HTTP 413 IF ANY file tripped a quota (so the client knows to prune), otherwise HTTP 200. get.description:
the public map of projects; no auth by design. THE PER-IP CEILING IS PART OF THE ROUTE, not a decoration on it (ADR 0252 §5.3). This GET is unauthenticated and CORS-open, and it was unmetered by construction: the two global limiters return early for reads, and the /public/* read limiter is mounted on a prefix this route does not sit under. It is also the platform's most expensive anonymous read — a cold cache turns one request into as many as 500 rows × 4 outbound fetches at OTHER PEOPLE's servers, so leaving it open aims our fan-out, not just our database. Auto-appear removed the old bound (the set of projects the operator had provisioned) and replaced it with "whoever points a domain at us", which is what makes the ceiling load-bearing rather than prudent. It runs BEFORE the handler, so a refused read costs no query and no fetch. PAGING DOES NOT RAISE THE CEILING IT SITS UNDER (task 1003561, absorbing task 1003560). `?limit=` only ever SHRINKS a page — parsePagination clamps it to the same 500 that used to be a silent hard truncation — so no request can aim more fan-out than one could before. `?offset=` reaches further down the catalog, and the only thing that costs is origins project-stats.js would have cached anyway: its 10-minute per-origin TTL, not the request count, is what bounds total outbound traffic. What paging BUYS is that the 501st project stops being invisible with nothing on the wire saying so.

**Rank:** `public` — No authentication — any caller.

The wizard's audience is any signed-in GitHub user, typically a xenos who used to get 403 on their own project. A caller who is neither gets the unchanged permission refusal, identical whether or not the project exists. IT WRITES NOTHING (task 1002818, ADR 0353). It used to pre-seed a 'pending' hub membership, but the hub holds no verdict: that row let nobody in, and on any door but `open` (new projects default to `apply`) the invitee who signed in met a locked door. Only the project's own invite admits (ADR 0335 D1/D2), so the answer is 200 `{ invited: false, invite_url }` — the project's hall invite box with the login pre-filled. A 200, not a refusal: it is the answer every admitted caller gets, and a 4xx on the normal path would log a failed request in the owner's browser on every invite. patch.description:
── The optional project detail (task 1002334, goal 1000046) ────────────── PATCH /provisioning/instances/:id/detail — answer (or re-answer) the wizard's OPTIONAL creation steps after creation. Body: any subset of { description, detail, modules }. rank: any authenticated builder (own resource; archon may change any — same gate as settings). THIS ROUTE IS WHAT MAKES THE STEP SKIPPABLE. Skipping at creation leaves the project dark-matter — off the map and un-joinable (ADR 0182 D4) — and that is a supported default only because there is a way back. Without this route "optional" would mean "permanently unpublishable", i.e. a dead end, which is precisely what criterion `proj-detail-interview` refuses. Deliberately NOT a settings-apply: nothing here is a policy the running instance obeys, so there is no web.env to patch and no restart to queue. The answers live on the platform row until a catalog row materializes (the provisioning_007 `type` precedent), and R16 (task 1002335) is the surface that reads `description` to compute publishability and name what is still missing. `modules` rides the SAME route for the same reason (BV1.R23, task 1002342, ADR 0245): step 4 of the wizard is skippable exactly as step 3 is, so it needs the same way back, and it lands on the same platform row under the same ownership gate. Only an ARRAY is a change — an omitted or null key leaves the column alone, so the "never asked" NULL (ADR 0240 §2) can never be written by a later edit. The always-on core stays unremovable by construction: badModuleSelection refuses its keys and `effectiveModules` re-adds it on read. `type` RIDES IT TOO (task 1003504), and for the third time the same argument: the wizard's Type step declared something at creation and nothing owner-facing could change it afterwards, so task 1002772 had to narrow the wizard's own promise and stop saying "you can change it later". This is the route that earns the sentence back. It belongs here rather than on the settings channel for the mModules reason — a type is a DECLARATION on the platform row, not a policy the running instance obeys, so nothing is pushed to the project and nothing restarts. One consequence is worth naming, because the owner has to be told it: for a project whose picker was SKIPPED, `modules` is NULL and effectiveModules resolves the type's starter bundle at read time (ADR 0240 §2) — so changing the type moves the extras too. A set the owner picked for themselves is stored and never moves. The reply carries `modules` on every patch precisely so the caller learns which happened without a follow-up GET. AN ANSWER CAN BE TAKEN BACK (task 1003577). `detail` merges, so before this the first `team_shape` an owner sent was permanent — and "never answered" is a state `effectiveModules` reads (ADR 0240), not merely the absence of one. Sending `detail: { <key>: null }` UN-ANSWERS that question: the key is dropped from the jsonb, so the row reads back exactly as one that was never asked and the bundle the answer moved moves back. Only null does it — an empty string or any other value is still refused as off-vocabulary, and `detail: {}` still changes nothing, because a form that collected no answers is not asking for any to be erased.

It lives here rather than at a module-catalog route because the two things a picker needs — what is preselected and what may be chosen — have to arrive in ONE read of ONE declaration, or the panel can preselect a key it has no row for. Core's limiter isn't reachable from a module (the one-way import rule; and the kernel doorway may not re-export it — it's a non-kernel core file, ADR 0091 §1), so we apply a dedicated, tight in-module limiter (askRateLimit). Descriptive analytics for the Archon-only scouting view — never authority. Optional `Bongos-Report-As-Of` header (task 1004268): when the instance read these totals, so an older report landing last cannot overwrite a newer one. A HEADER, not a body field, because the body is validated strictly and the hub and its instances upgrade independently: a new instance's body field would 400 on an older hub and the report would be lost, while an unknown header is ignored. Absent or unparseable reads as unstamped (last-writer-wins, as before) rather than a 400 — the sender never reads the response, so a refusal would silently drop the report instead of only its ordering. rank: public — authenticated by client_id + client_secret, not a builder rank.

POST /sso/applicant-profile — a federated instance resolves ONE applicant's profile view for its own reviewer queue, LIVE at render (privacy spec D7, task 1002972). Server-to-server, client_id+client_secret auth, like the two routes above. Answers { profile: null | { view:'public', … } | { view: 'sliver', … }, guild } — the D7 rule, decided entirely inside ../applicant-profile.js, plus the guild the applicant applied with (ADR 0365 D5): { slug, name } while they are still a member of it (slug null for an unlisted guild), else null. A project on an older core reads only `profile` and ignores the rest (the ADR 0201 D2.2 compatibility rule). WHY A POST FOR A READ. The same reason /sso/activity/rollup is one: the credentials are in the body, and a client_secret in a query string lands in access logs and proxy history. Nothing is written. THE ECHO IS THE GATE, AND IT IS THE WHOLE SECURITY ARGUMENT (ADR 0205, security report 1000027). Client credentials prove WHICH PROJECT is calling and nothing about WHO the github_id is, so authenticating the caller is not enough: without a per-subject witness this route is a bulk disclosure oracle over every account on the platform, private ones included, readable by any registered project holding only its own secret. applicationBacksProfileRead demands a HUB-WRITTEN echo for exactly (this account, this client) inside the 30-day window — a row only the hub's own join relay creates, and only after the project accepted the relayed application. A project may therefore read the profile of someone who applied TO IT, and of nobody else. 404, never 403, when the echo is absent — the /scouting/:handle posture. A 403 would confirm that the github_id names a real account, which is the disclosure the whole rule exists to withhold. An account that exists but discloses nothing (provisional, terms never accepted) answers the SAME { profile: null } as one that consented but is simply not readable, so the caller cannot tell those apart either (ADR 0171 D4). NOT AUTHORITY (ADR 0016). The answer is descriptive; the project's own admission gate reads status='invited' and never this. rank: public — authenticated by client_id + client_secret, not a builder rank. The limiter runs BEFORE the client lookup, so a refused probe costs no DB work — the accountExistenceReadRateLimit posture.

The client_id is taken from the AUTHENTICATED client — the caller cannot report membership for a project it doesn't hold the secret for. So this route may neither create a membership nor rewrite an account's identity: it updates a row the HUB already witnessed a sign-in for (signin_verified_at, stamped only at /sso/token and /sso/device/poll), and it creates the account shell only when absent. The second is a predicate over tasks.created_by, which no rank floor can express — the ADR 0151 ownership axis, and this is its first route. requirePermission structurally cannot carry it: an own-scoped key has no unconditional answer and that gate refuses one outright (auth.js, R100), so `.own` can never collapse into `.any`. The two facts are resolved in two places ON PURPOSE. The RANK fact is request-scoped and resolves here, once, uncached (ADR 0016); the OWNER fact is a column that can change under us, so it is evaluated inside abandonTask's FOR UPDATE transaction. Reading created_by here would be a TOCTOU window; resolving permissions in there would hold a row lock across a second pool acquire. Existing guards (shipped refused, active claim refused, idempotent re-abandon) and the audit_log entry are unchanged on both paths.

Without this, an ENFORCING ADR-0058 gate-review BLOCKS a Metic+ author's gate-surface PR shipped from a laptop and they can't self-approve their own PR (hit live on task 1162 / PR task 131). The attestation power is bounded: gate-author-trust clears a NEEDS_TRUST surface for a Metic+ author only and NEVER the hard floor (which always needs an owner review), so a Metic+ vouching for their own task's head stays within their tier.

The endpoint validates+scores the JSON, writes the task_grades row, and — if both functional_fidelity and code_quality clear threshold — promotes the task from completed→confirmed and awards credits. Supervisor hot path (preserved per CRITICAL §4 — no requireRank).

A thing with no closing move does not close, which is how two versions ended up building at once. Archon-only, behind the `version.close` permission that has existed at that floor since BV1.R105 and that, until now, NOTHING referenced. THE TWO-STEP IS R14's ARCHIVE, in spirit and in shape: call it bare and a version holding open goals refuses with the GOALS ATTACHED; re-submit with a total `dispositions` map and it closes. Agents already know that interaction, and a second idiom for the same thing is how two surfaces drift apart. Auto-close (task 1003603, R16) reaches `db.closeVersion` with an EMPTY plan and never touches this route: by construction it fires only when the last non-maintenance goal achieved, so nothing is left to disposition (ADR 0263 §3). rank: archon — the disposition that finalises a version's scope-truth.

post.description:
Auth (Metic+, then the goal's own authority): create a done-when criterion at RUNTIME. ADR 0105 moved scope-truth seeds (versions/goals/criteria) out of the normal migration path, so a brand-new criterion on a RUNNING instance can no longer be added by a plain migration (migrations/instance/ applies only under the owner opt-in GDS_APPLY_INSTANCE_SEEDS=1, a DR step). This is the vector a planning session uses to add a criterion to a live version WITHOUT a droplet migrate. ADR 0154 — authority over a GOAL's criteria follows GOAL OWNERSHIP, not global rank. A Metic who may create the goal (POST /goals) and author the tasks under it (POST /tasks, ADR 0090) may now write the criteria those tasks gate — but only inside a goal they own or manage. Deliberately NOT a flat re-rank: - An unsatisfied criterion permanently blocks version close (version-close.js counts satisfied === total per VERSION, regardless of goal) and goal auto-achieve (db.achieveGoalIfComplete). There is NO delete route, so it cannot be undone via the API — the same backward ratchet as unsatisfy, which stays Archon. - So a non-Archon must name a goal_id (version-level criteria stay Archon), must be that goal's OWNER or MANAGER (isGoalOwnerOrManager — the same predicate behind visibility/invite/membership management), and the goal must be open on a planning/building version. That bounds the blast radius to a workspace they already hold. An unauthorized caller gets an honest 403 goal_not_yours (task 1002614 — goal reads are open to any builder, so there is no existence oracle for a mask to protect). Pinned in route-rank-check.MODULE_EXPECTED_RANKS. rank: metic+archon — criterion create, walled by goal ownership (ADR 0154).

code.description: Stable machine-readable slug the caller may switch on (e.g. `task_not_found`). Classified into a category (`x-error-categories`); the specific slug is preserved (ADR 0116).

message.description: Human-readable, safe to surface. Never leaks internals unless a handler opts in.

details.description: Optional structured payload — e.g. the validator's `[{ field, reason }]` list.

ApiErrorObject.description: The inner error object carried by every non-2xx response.

ErrorEnvelope.description: The single error shape returned by EVERY non-2xx response (ADR 0116). A caller reads `error.code`.

limit.description: Page size actually applied (clamped to the endpoint cap, ADR 0119).

offset.description: Zero-based row offset of this page.

total.description: Total matching rows, when cheaply countable; derive "more pages" via `offset + items.length < total`.

PageInfo.description: The `page` block of a paginated list response (ADR 0119), built by `pageMeta()`.

StringifiableId.description: A resource id — an integer, or its stringified form (a Postgres bigint serializes as a JSON string, so ids may arrive either way). Accept both.

BadRequest.description: Malformed or invalid request (the ADR-0116 error envelope).

not_found.description: The referenced resource does not exist.
